title: Congestive Heart Failure
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Heart failure is a syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood for tissue needs, or can do so only at abnormally high filling pressures. Nearly every finding comes from congestion behind the failing ventricle (backward failure), inadequate flow ahead of it (forward failure), or the neurohormonal response to both. This chapter moves from left-sided and right-sided findings to reduced versus preserved ejection fraction, the compensations that drive progression, the complications, high-output failure, and acute mitral regurgitation. Board questions usually describe a patient and ask you to place the lesion (left or right, systolic or diastolic, low or high output) or predict the next consequence, so the emphasis is on mechanism.
prerequisites: Determinants of stroke volume and the Frank-Starling relationship (CV-6)
Pressure-volume loops and the phases of the cardiac cycle (CV-4, CV-6)
Starling forces across capillaries and the role of lymphatics (CV-10, CV-11)
Baroreceptor reflex and renal handling of sodium and water, renin, aldosterone, and ADH (CV-11, renal physiology)
Hepatic acinus zones and their blood supply (GI histology)

connections.how: Loss of contracting muscle after infarction is the most common cause of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.
Long-standing hypertension produces concentric hypertrophy and is the leading cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and pulmonary hypertension produces cor pulmonale.

connections.to: Valvular heart diseases and primary myocardial diseases (CV-18-D, CV-18-E)
connections.how: Pressure and volume overload from valve lesions and intrinsic muscle disease from cardiomyopathies are the other main roads to a failing ventricle.
Thiamine deficiency causes wet beriberi, a high-output failure rooted in failed oxidative metabolism.
The kidney reads low cardiac output as low blood volume, so its sodium and water retention is the engine of edema and of cardiorenal syndrome.

terms.def: A syndrome in which the heart cannot deliver enough blood for tissue needs, or does so only at elevated filling pressures.
The congestion and edema that result when pressure rises in the chamber and veins behind a failing ventricle.
The consequences of inadequate cardiac output, such as fatigue, renal hypoperfusion, and confusion.
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (40% or lower), caused mainly by impaired contraction (systolic dysfunction).
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (50% or higher), caused mainly by impaired relaxation and filling (diastolic dysfunction).
Dyspnea that appears when lying flat and is relieved by sitting up.
Sudden breathlessness that wakes a patient from sleep, typically one to a few hours after lying down.
Alveolar macrophages that have engulfed red cells and stored their iron as hemosiderin, a sign of chronic pulmonary congestion.
Right ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, or failure caused by pulmonary hypertension from disease of the lungs or pulmonary vessels, not from left heart disease or congenital heart disease.
The gross appearance of chronic passive hepatic congestion: dark red congested centrilobular areas alternating with paler periportal tissue.
The portion of blood volume that the arterial baroreceptors and kidney sense as filling the arterial tree; it falls in heart failure even when total volume is expanded.
Congestive failure in which cardiac output is above normal but still inadequate, usually because systemic vascular resistance is low or metabolic demand is high.

sections.title: Left-sided heart failure: causes and the consequences of pulmonary venous congestion

blocks.text: When the left ventricle cannot empty in systole or fill at a normal pressure in diastole, its end-diastolic pressure rises. The open mitral valve passes that pressure to the left atrium, and the valveless pulmonary veins pass it on to the pulmonary capillaries, so left-sided failure shows itself first in the lungs.
Causes

Ischemic heart disease is the most common cause, through loss of muscle after infarction and through chronic ischemia. Systemic hypertension and aortic stenosis add a pressure load that first produces concentric hypertrophy and impaired filling, aortic and mitral regurgitation add a volume load that dilates the ventricle, and cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, sustained tachyarrhythmias, alcohol, and anthracyclines damage or stiffen the muscle directly. Mitral stenosis and left atrial myxoma produce every pulmonary sign below while the left ventricle stays normal or underfilled.
From raised left atrial pressure to pulmonary edema

Normal pulmonary capillary pressure is about 7 mmHg against a plasma oncotic pressure of about 28 mmHg, so lymphatics easily clear the small net filtration. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) approximates left atrial pressure and is normally about 6 to 12 mmHg. As it rises, fluid collects first in the interstitium around vessels and small airways, and once capillary pressure exceeds roughly the plasma oncotic pressure and filtration outruns lymph flow, fluid floods the alveoli. A low plasma albumin lowers this threshold. The rate of rise matters as much as the level: in chronic failure or mitral stenosis the lymphatics enlarge and carry many times their normal flow, so a wedge pressure that causes frank edema after an acute infarct may be tolerated.
Dyspnea, orthopnea, and PND

Interstitial fluid stiffens the lungs and stimulates juxtacapillary (J) receptors that drive rapid, shallow breathing, and alveolar fluid adds ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia; bronchial wall edema can cause wheeze (cardiac asthma). Lying flat shifts several hundred milliliters of blood from the legs and splanchnic veins into the thorax, and a failing ventricle on the flat part of its Frank-Starling curve turns that extra preload into higher capillary pressure. PND appears one to a few hours after lying down, because edema fluid from the legs is reabsorbed while sympathetic support and respiratory center sensitivity fall during sleep.

blocks.title: From a failing left ventricle to orthopnea and PND

Left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise

Stiff lungs and J receptor stimulation: dyspnea on exertion
Lying flat shifts blood into the chest: orthopnea
Leg edema reabsorbed during sleep: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea

blocks.caption: Each step adds central volume or pressure that a failing left ventricle cannot absorb, so congestion worsens in a predictable order.

blocks.text: Crackles, heart failure cells, and forward findings

Fine late inspiratory crackles come from fluid-filled small airways snapping open and begin at the bases, where capillary hydrostatic pressure is highest. Pleural effusions are transudates and often bilateral. In chronic congestion, red cells leak into the alveoli and alveolar macrophages store their iron as hemosiderin, which stains with Prussian blue; these heart failure cells lie in the lung and sputum, and with septal fibrosis they give brown induration. Forward failure adds fatigue, cool pale extremities, confusion in older patients, and prerenal azotemia, with a BUN to creatinine ratio above about 20 because enhanced proximal and ADH-driven urea reabsorption accompany the fall in filtration.

sections.title: Right-sided heart failure: causes and the consequences of systemic venous congestion

blocks.text: The thin-walled right ventricle handles volume loads well but fails quickly against a high afterload. Its failure raises right atrial pressure, which passes into the venae cavae and every systemic venous bed.
Causes

Left-sided failure is the most common cause. Chronically raised pulmonary venous pressure raises pulmonary artery pressure, first passively and then through arteriolar remodeling, and the right ventricle hypertrophies, dilates, and fails (biventricular failure). Cor pulmonale is right ventricular failure from pulmonary hypertension arising in the lungs or pulmonary vessels. Acute cor pulmonale follows massive pulmonary embolism, and chronic cor pulmonale follows chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, interstitial lung disease, hypoventilation syndromes, pulmonary arterial hypertension, and chronic thromboembolic disease, largely through hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and later medial hypertrophy. Right ventricular infarction, which accompanies an inferior infarct from proximal right coronary occlusion, causes hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs, because less blood reaches the left ventricle and the dilated right ventricle shifts the septum leftward.
Neck veins and pitting edema

The right internal jugular vein acts as a manometer for right atrial pressure, which normally averages about 0 to 6 mmHg. With the patient at about 45 degrees, a pulsation more than about 3 to 4 cm above the sternal angle indicates raised pressure. In hepatojugular reflux, abdominal pressure for about 10 to 15 seconds pushes splanchnic blood toward the right heart; a failing right ventricle cannot accept it, so the JVP stays up while pressure is held.

Dependent edema needs both raised venous pressure, which increases capillary filtration, and renal sodium and water retention, which supplies the volume. Several liters accumulate before swelling is visible, so weight gain comes first. The edema settles at the ankles in ambulatory patients and the sacrum in bedridden ones, and it pits because it is a low-protein transudate, unlike lymphedema or the myxedema of hypothyroidism.
Nutmeg liver

Raised hepatic venous pressure distends the central veins and centrilobular sinusoids. Zone 3 hepatocytes, farthest from portal inflow, become hypoxic and atrophy, while zone 1 may show fatty change, which gives the dark red and tan nutmeg pattern. Low output added to congestion causes centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, and years of congestion cause centrilobular fibrosis (cardiac sclerosis). The liver is enlarged and tender, and congestion also produces ascites, congestive splenomegaly, and bowel wall edema with anorexia.

blocks.predict: A patient with an inferior myocardial infarction is hypotensive, has a JVP 9 cm above the sternal angle, and has clear lung fields. Predict what has happened to left ventricular filling.
blocks.explain: Left ventricular filling is reduced. A right ventricular infarction lowers right ventricular output, so less blood crosses the lungs to the left heart, and the dilated right ventricle shifts the septum leftward. Systemic venous pressure rises while pulmonary venous pressure does not, which is why the neck veins are full and the lungs are clear.

sections.title: Reduced versus preserved ejection fraction, and the S3, BNP, and chest radiograph

blocks.text: Ejection fraction (EF) is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally about 55% to 70%. HFrEF (EF 40% or lower) is mainly a failure of contraction, HFpEF (EF 50% or higher) is mainly a failure of relaxation and filling, and an EF of 41% to 49% is called mildly reduced. Both raise filling pressure, so both cause the same congestion.
HFrEF: a weak, dilated ventricle

After infarction or in dilated cardiomyopathy, the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship flattens, so the ventricle ejects less and keeps a larger end-systolic volume. It compensates by adding sarcomeres in series (eccentric hypertrophy) and using the Frank-Starling mechanism at a larger end-diastolic volume. By the law of Laplace, wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, so the dilated ventricle has high wall stress, high oxygen demand, and a stretched mitral annulus that may leak (functional mitral regurgitation).
HFpEF: a stiff ventricle that empties normally

Active relaxation requires ATP to return Ca2+ to the sarcoplasmic reticulum through SERCA2a and to release cross-bridges, so ischemia, hypertrophy, and aging slow it. Passive stiffness rises with concentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel), fibrosis, titin changes, and infiltration such as amyloid. The end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship steepens, so even a normal volume requires a high diastolic pressure. HFpEF is most common in older adults, women, and patients with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation. The stiff ventricle depends on atrial contraction, so atrial fibrillation or a fast rate that shortens diastole can tip it into pulmonary edema.

blocks.text: S3, BNP, and the chest radiograph

The S3 is a low-pitched early diastolic sound at the apex, produced when rapid filling from a high-pressure atrium is suddenly halted by a dilated ventricle near its limit of distension. It marks volume overload and high filling pressure, classically in HFrEF, and is normal in children, young adults, athletes, and pregnancy. The S4 is a late diastolic sound from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle and disappears in atrial fibrillation.

BNP is released from stretched ventricular myocytes as proBNP, which is cleaved into active BNP and inactive NT-proBNP. BNP raises cGMP through the NPR-A receptor and is cleared by neprilysin and NPR-C, while NT-proBNP is cleared mainly by the kidney. A BNP below about 100 pg/mL or an NT-proBNP below about 300 pg/mL makes acute heart failure unlikely. Levels rise with age, renal failure, atrial fibrillation, and right ventricular strain, fall with obesity, and are lower in HFpEF because a thick wall lowers wall stress for a given pressure.
Radiographic signs follow pulmonary venous pressure in a set order, and cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 on a posteroanterior film) supports a dilated heart but is often absent in HFpEF.

blocks.title: Chest radiograph signs as wedge pressure rises
steps: Normal, about 6 to 12 mmHg: lower-lobe vessels larger than upper
About 13 to 18 mmHg: upper-lobe diversion (cephalization)
About 18 to 25 mmHg: Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing, hazy hila
Above about 25 mmHg: perihilar bat-wing alveolar opacities
blocks.caption: Signs lag behind rapid pressure changes and appear at higher pressures in chronic failure because lymphatic drainage has increased.

sections.title: Neurohormonal compensation: support that becomes the disease

blocks.text: The baroreceptors and kidney cannot tell a failing pump from hemorrhage, so a fall in cardiac output triggers the same defense: sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Total extracellular volume is expanded, yet effective arterial blood volume is low, so these systems stay switched on.
Sympathetic activation, RAAS, and ADH

Reduced baroreceptor firing raises sympathetic outflow: beta-1 stimulation raises heart rate and contractility, alpha-1 arteriolar constriction holds arterial pressure, and venoconstriction raises preload. Over months, catecholamines raise oxygen demand and afterload, cause Ca2+ overload, arrhythmias, and myocyte death, and downregulate beta-1 receptors through receptor kinases and beta-arrestin.

Renin is released in response to low afferent arteriolar pressure, low macula densa NaCl delivery, and renal beta-1 stimulation. Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors to constrict arterioles, constrict the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, increase proximal Na+ reabsorption, stimulate thirst and ADH, and release aldosterone, which drives Na+ reabsorption in collecting duct principal cells at the cost of K+ and H+. On a flat Frank-Starling curve the retained volume adds little stroke volume and mostly raises venous pressure. Baroreceptor-driven (nonosmotic) ADH release adds aquaporin-2 water retention through V2 receptors, so hyponatremia marks advanced disease.

blocks.title: The neurohormonal cycle of heart failure
steps: Myocardial injury lowers cardiac output and arterial filling
Baroreceptors and the kidney sense low effective arterial volume
Sympathetic activation, renin release, and nonosmotic ADH release
Short-term support: higher heart rate, contractility, vascular tone, and blood volume
Vasoconstriction raises afterload; salt and water retention raise preload beyond benefit, causing congestion
Catecholamines, angiotensin II, and aldosterone cause myocyte loss, hypertrophy, and fibrosis
Remodeling lowers pump function further, which lowers output again
blocks.caption: A response designed for hemorrhage, sustained for months, worsens the pump it is trying to support.

blocks.text: Remodeling and natriuretic peptides

Remodeling is the progressive change in ventricular size, shape, and composition after injury: myocytes enlarge and re-express fetal genes, some die by apoptosis, and angiotensin II and aldosterone drive fibrosis. In HFrEF the ventricle becomes larger and more spherical, which raises wall stress and pulls the papillary muscles apart, so the process becomes self-sustaining. Blocking beta-1 receptors, angiotensin II, or aldosterone slows remodeling but raising contractility alone does not, so the hormones themselves drive progression. ANP from atria and BNP from ventricles oppose these systems through NPR-A and cGMP, but receptor downregulation, neprilysin, and low renal perfusion blunt their effect.

Little gain once the curve flattens; congestion and edema

Maintained arterial pressure and glomerular filtration
Higher afterload, sodium retention, hypertrophy, fibrosis

blocks.caption: Every compensation in the upper rows is helpful in a short crisis and harmful when sustained; natriuretic peptides are the only one that pushes the other way.

blocks.predict: Predict the serum sodium and the urine sodium of a patient with advanced heart failure and marked edema.
blocks.explain: Serum sodium tends to be low because nonosmotic ADH release retains water in excess of sodium. Urine sodium is low because angiotensin II and aldosterone avidly reabsorb filtered sodium. The body is overloaded with both sodium and water, yet the kidney behaves as if the patient were volume depleted, because it senses low effective arterial volume.

blocks.text: Complications follow from high filling pressures, low forward output, or enlarged, scarred, neurohormonally stimulated chambers.
Acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock

Acute pulmonary edema occurs when left atrial pressure rises faster than lymphatics can adapt, triggered by ischemia, a hypertensive surge, a fast arrhythmia, acute valve regurgitation, or a sudden salt load. It produces severe dyspnea, diffuse crackles, frothy pink sputum, and hypoxemia, and the sympathetic surge it provokes raises afterload further. The same picture at a normal wedge pressure suggests noncardiogenic edema, as in acute respiratory distress syndrome.

Cardiogenic shock is hypoperfusion from pump failure: systolic pressure below about 90 mmHg for at least 30 minutes, cardiac index below about 2.2 L/min/m2, and wedge pressure above about 15 to 18 mmHg. It classically follows infarction of 40% or more of the left ventricle. The patient is cold and wet, with low mixed venous oxygen saturation and lactic acidosis, and hypotension lowers coronary perfusion, which worsens ischemia. Its profile is low output, high wedge pressure, and high systemic vascular resistance (SVR); hypovolemic shock shares low output and high SVR but has a low wedge pressure, and early septic shock has high output with low SVR.
Arrhythmias

Atrial stretch and angiotensin II and aldosterone driven fibrosis promote atrial fibrillation, which removes the atrial kick and shortens diastole, and persistently fast rates can cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. Ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation cause many sudden deaths: scar supports reentry, fewer repolarizing K+ channels prolong the action potential and favor early afterdepolarizations, catecholamines and Ca2+ overload favor delayed afterdepolarizations, and hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia destabilize repolarization.
Mural thrombi, cardiorenal syndrome, and cachexia

Virchow's triad explains mural thrombi: stasis in a dilated ventricle, akinetic segment, or fibrillating left atrial appendage, endocardial injury over an infarct, and a procoagulant state. Thrombi show lines of Zahn and embolize to the brain, gut, kidneys, spleen, and limbs.

In cardiorenal syndrome, low output and renal vasoconstriction reduce renal flow, while raised central venous pressure raises renal venous and interstitial pressure inside the capsule and lowers the gradient for filtration. Creatinine and BUN rise, and the added sodium retention worsens congestion. Cardiac cachexia comes from TNF alpha and interleukin-6 driven proteolysis, gut congestion with anorexia and malabsorption, and higher energy expenditure, and edema can hide the weight loss.

In high-output heart failure, cardiac output is above normal, yet the patient has congestion and edema. The defining feature is low systemic vascular resistance (SVR) from arteriolar vasodilation, arteriovenous shunting, or high metabolic demand.
Why low resistance produces congestion

Mean arterial pressure is approximately cardiac output times SVR, so a fall in SVR lowers arterial pressure unless output rises. The baroreceptors and kidney sense arterial underfilling, exactly as in low-output failure, and sympathetic activation, RAAS, and ADH retain sodium and water. Blood volume, venous return, and output rise. A normal heart sustains this for a time, but the persistent volume and rate load eventually raises filling pressures and dilates the ventricles, and a diseased heart reaches that point sooner.

blocks.title: Arteriovenous fistula and the cardiac output equation
blocks.text: With a mean arterial pressure of about 93 mmHg and a cardiac output of 5 L/min, SVR is about 18.6 mmHg per L/min (Wood units). A large dialysis fistula adds a low-resistance channel in parallel and lowers total SVR to about 10 Wood units. To keep mean arterial pressure near 90 mmHg, cardiac output must rise to about 9 L/min. Much of this extra flow passes through the fistula without reaching capillaries, so tissues gain little, venous blood returns well oxygenated, and the heart carries the extra work. Compressing the fistula raises SVR and arterial pressure, and the baroreflex slows the heart (the Nicoladoni-Branham sign).
Causes

Severe anemia causes hypoxic vasodilation and lowers blood viscosity. Thyrotoxicosis raises metabolic demand and heat dissipation, and T3 relaxes vascular smooth muscle while increasing SERCA2a, alpha myosin heavy chain, and beta-1 receptors and decreasing phospholamban. Wet beriberi is thiamine deficiency: thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, so ATP production falls, arterioles dilate, and the energy-starved myocardium dilates; Shoshin beriberi is the fulminant form with lactic acidosis. Extensive Paget disease creates hypervascular bone that behaves like many shunts. Pregnancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, severe obesity, and some myeloproliferative disorders also produce high-output states.

blocks.predict: A patient on hemodialysis develops orthopnea and edema. Cardiac output is 9 L/min and mixed venous oxygen saturation is high. Predict the SVR and explain the oxygen finding.
blocks.explain: SVR is low because the dialysis fistula provides a low-resistance path from artery to vein. A large fraction of the output passes through the fistula without unloading oxygen in capillaries, so venous blood returning to the heart is well saturated.

sections.title: Acute mitral regurgitation from chordal or papillary muscle rupture

blocks.text: Chordae tendineae anchored to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles keep the mitral leaflets closed in systole. If a chord or papillary muscle ruptures, part of a leaflet flails into the left atrium and a large regurgitant jet appears within seconds.
Causes

Chordal rupture occurs with myxomatous degeneration (mitral valve prolapse), infective endocarditis, blunt chest trauma, and less often rheumatic disease. Papillary muscle rupture complicates myocardial infarction about 3 to 7 days after the infarct, when necrotic muscle has been removed before collagen forms. The posteromedial muscle, usually supplied only by the posterior descending artery, ruptures with inferior infarcts (CV-18-C). Rupture of a whole trunk is usually rapidly fatal, while rupture of one head can be survivable.
Hemodynamics and findings

The ventricle now ejects into both the aorta and the low-pressure left atrium, from the start of systole. The normal-sized, noncompliant atrium cannot absorb the volume, so its pressure rises steeply (giant v wave) and causes sudden pulmonary edema. The undilated ventricle cannot raise total stroke volume enough, so forward output falls into cardiogenic shock, and sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts still more flow backward. Because atrial pressure approaches ventricular pressure in late systole, the murmur may be early systolic, decrescendo, soft, or absent, and heart size on radiograph is normal. Ventricular septal rupture presents similarly but gives a loud holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and an oxygen saturation step-up from right atrium to right ventricle.

blocks.title: Rupture of a chord or papillary muscle to shock
steps: Chord or papillary muscle ruptures; a leaflet flails into the left atrium
Large regurgitant volume enters a small, noncompliant left atrium each systole
Left atrial pressure rises steeply (giant v wave)
Pulmonary capillary pressure rises abruptly: acute pulmonary edema
Forward stroke volume falls because the undilated ventricle cannot raise total output
Hypotension and cardiogenic shock; sympathetic vasoconstriction diverts more flow backward
blocks.caption: The suddenness of the lesion, not its size alone, explains the severity of the presentation.

blocks.title: Why the ejection fraction looks normal in shock
blocks.text: Before rupture: end-diastolic volume 120 mL, end-systolic volume 50 mL, stroke volume 70 mL, EF 58%, heart rate 72 per minute, cardiac output about 5.0 L/min. After rupture, the ventricle also empties into the low-pressure atrium, so end-systolic volume falls to 30 mL. Total stroke volume is 90 mL and EF is 75%. But if 50 mL of each beat goes into the left atrium (a regurgitant fraction, the backward share of total stroke volume, of about 56%), forward stroke volume is only 40 mL. Even at a heart rate of 100 per minute, forward output is 4.0 L/min, and 50 mL per beat entering a small atrium drives the wedge pressure sharply upward. EF overstates forward performance in mitral regurgitation.

blocks.title: Acute compared with chronic mitral regurgitation
rows: Very high, with giant v waves
Maintained for years by a larger total stroke volume
Early systolic, decrescendo, may be soft or absent
Enlarged left atrium and left ventricle
Atrial fibrillation common from atrial dilation
blocks.caption: Chronic compensation, atrial dilation and eccentric ventricular hypertrophy, is exactly what the acute lesion lacks.

integration.text: The two hearts are pumps in series, so failure of either side backs pressure into the veins that drain into it and reduces flow beyond it. Starling forces and lymphatic capacity decide when that pressure becomes edema, the law of Laplace explains high wall stress in a dilated ventricle and lower BNP in a thick one, and the hepatic acinus explains why congestion injures zone 3. The same hormones that normally regulate sodium and water now respond to a falsely low effective arterial volume, and their receptors (AT1, mineralocorticoid, V2, NPR-A) are where the cycle can be interrupted.

Pathology and microbiology supply causes and tissue findings: infarct repair sets the timing of papillary muscle rupture, Virchow's triad explains mural thrombi, and coxsackie B myocarditis, Chagas disease, rheumatic heart disease, and endocarditis are infectious routes to failure. Every marker has mechanistic limits: EF overstates forward output in mitral regurgitation, BNP rises in renal failure and falls in obesity, radiographic signs lag behind pressure, and an S3 is normal in the young.

summary: Heart failure is inadequate output, or adequate output only at high filling pressure; findings reflect backward congestion, forward hypoperfusion, and neurohormonal activation.
Left-sided failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure, causing edema, dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, basal crackles, and heart failure cells; mitral stenosis does this with a normal left ventricle.

Left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure; cor pulmonale arises from lung or pulmonary vascular disease, and right ventricular infarction gives hypotension, raised JVP, and clear lungs.
Right-sided failure raises systemic venous pressure: raised JVP, sustained hepatojugular reflux, dependent pitting edema, ascites, and nutmeg liver from zone 3 hypoxia.
HFrEF (EF 40% or lower) is a weak, dilated ventricle with an S3; HFpEF (EF 50% or higher) is a stiff, thick ventricle with an S4; both raise filling pressure.
BNP reflects ventricular wall stress; a low level makes acute heart failure unlikely, and radiographs progress from cephalization to Kerley B lines to bat-wing alveolar edema.

Sympathetic activation, RAAS, and nonosmotic ADH defend arterial pressure but raise afterload, retain sodium and water, cause hyponatremia, and drive remodeling; natriuretic peptides cannot overcome them.
Complications follow from high pressure, low flow, or damaged chambers: pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, mural thrombi, cardiorenal syndrome, and cachexia.
High-output failure (anemia, thyrotoxicosis, arteriovenous fistula, wet beriberi, Paget disease) has low SVR, warm extremities, wide pulse pressure, and normal or high mixed venous saturation.
Acute mitral regurgitation loads a small, stiff left atrium, causing giant v waves, sudden pulmonary edema, low forward output despite a normal EF, and a murmur that may be soft.

verify: Ejection fraction cutoffs (40% or lower for HFrEF, 41% to 49% mildly reduced, 50% or higher for HFpEF) follow current consensus guideline classification; confirm the categories and names NABNE uses.
BNP and NT-proBNP rule-out thresholds (about 100 pg/mL and about 300 pg/mL for acute heart failure) come from guideline consensus and vary with assay, age, and setting.
Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure bands for radiographic stages (about 13 to 18, 18 to 25, and above 25 mmHg) are approximate and differ slightly among radiology and physiology sources.
Pulmonary Starling force values (capillary pressure about 7 mmHg, plasma oncotic pressure about 28 mmHg) are Guyton and Hall values; other texts give slightly different numbers.

Normal JVP upper limit (about 3 to 4 cm above the sternal angle), normal mean right atrial pressure (about 0 to 6 mmHg), and the duration of abdominal pressure for hepatojugular reflux vary between clinical sources.
Cardiogenic shock criteria (systolic pressure below about 90 mmHg, cardiac index below about 2.2 L/min/m2, wedge pressure above about 15 to 18 mmHg) differ between trials and guidelines.
The 40% of left ventricular mass figure for cardiogenic shock after infarction is the classic Robbins value; confirm if tested.
The extent of skeletal involvement in Paget disease needed to cause high-output failure is not stated here because sources differ; confirm whether NABNE expects a figure.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Nicoladoni-Branham sign, Kerley B lines, lines of Zahn, and Shoshin beriberi, or only the descriptive terms.
